investigations.title: Flame Extinguishment Experiment

plain.text: FLEX burned small fuel droplets (methanol and heptane) aboard the International Space Station. It looked for the lowest oxygen level at which a flame can survive in weightlessness, and for how well gases such as carbon dioxide and helium put flames out. Hundreds of logged tests record each droplet's starting size, how fast it burned, and its size when the flame went out.

technical.text: Methanol (CH3OH) and heptane (C7H16) droplets, mostly free-floating, with initial diameters of 2 to 5 mm, were ignited in the MDCA within the CIR on the ISS. The ambients were O2/N2 with CO2 or He suppressants. The aim was to map flammability boundaries and determine the Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI) as a function of pressure and suppressant. Planned ranges were O2 mole fraction 0.10 to 0.50, suppressant 0.00 to the no-flame limit (0.70 expected) and pressure 0.5 to 1.0 atm; the approach states 0.5 − 1.5 atm. Test sheets span 0.70 to 3.05 atm. Some tests imposed a sub-buoyant flow by translating the droplet. Per-test outputs are D0, kavg (mm2/s) and Dext (mm), from HiBMS backlit imaging, LLUV and color cameras and a radiometer.

key_findings.text: A heptane droplet in 0.18/0.42/0.40 O2/N2/He at 0.70 atm (D0 1.86 mm) burned with kavg 0.77 mm2/s to Dext 0.84 mm. The test sheet describes this as likely diffusive extinction very close to the flammability limit, with no evidence of a cool flame.

A heptane droplet in air at 1.0 atm with D0 3.56 mm showed flame oscillations. These suggest the initial size was at the edge of the radiative limit, but the flame stabilized and burned to disruption.
Methanol droplets in air at 1.00 atm (D0 2.54 mm) burned with kavg 0.48 mm2/s and Dext 1.53 mm. In 0.18/0.67/0.15 O2/N2/CO2 at 1.00 atm (D0 3.77 mm), the values were kavg 0.42 mm2/s and Dext 1.79 mm.
A methanol droplet in 0.24/0.56/0.20 O2/N2/CO2 at 0.70 atm (D0 4.25 mm) had kavg 0.45 mm2/s and Dext 2.60 mm.
A methanol droplet in 0.30/0.70 O2/N2 at 1.01 atm (D0 3.26 mm) burned with kavg 0.59 mm2/s and extinguished at Dext 1.32 mm, becoming 'football'-shaped at extinction.

Methanol and heptane droplets are simple, well-characterized fuels, but they do not represent the practical solid fuels of fire safety studies such as PMMA or paper.

investigations.title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator

plain.text: BRE used a flat gas burner on the International Space Station to imitate how solid materials such as plastics burn when there is no airflow. Flames representing materials like PMMA and Nylon kept burning steadily in still air, especially in oxygen-rich atmospheres considered for future spacecraft. In normal air (21% oxygen), such flames went out quickly.

technical.text: ACME-BRE ran in the ACME hardware of the CIR on the ISS. It fed CH4/N2 and C2H4/N2 mixtures through flat porous circular burners of 25 and 50 mm diameter to emulate condensed-phase burning in a quiescent microgravity ambient. Fuel mixtures were chosen to represent real solids through heat of combustion, smoke point and heat of gasification. Each BRE burner carries two heat flux transducers and a surface thermocouple. The O2/N2 ambients were 14.7 psia, 21 % oxygen; 10.2 psia, 26.5 %; and 8.2 psia, 34 % oxygen, with O2/CO2 ambients desired. Flames first burned at fixed fuel flow while burner temperature and heat flux evolved. Flow was then reduced in increments until extinction, producing flammability-map data.

The card states that it yielded data relevant to spacecraft fire safety.

plain.text: BASS-II burned small samples of acrylic plastic and a cotton-fiberglass fabric inside a tiny wind tunnel on the International Space Station. The crew varied the airflow and lowered the oxygen level to find when flames spread, grow or go out in weightlessness. The aim was to help NASA judge whether Earth-based flammability tests are a safe guide for choosing spacecraft materials.

Variables: forced flow speed and direction (opposed and concurrent; up to 40 cm/s per the summary card, 5 to 50 cm/s per the fact sheet) and ambient O2 below 21% via nitrogen vitiation. Measured: ignition, flame appearance, growth, spread and regression rates, limiting flame length and extinction limits, using video and still imaging, an anemometer and a radiometer.

plain.text: BASS burned small samples of fabrics, plastics and candle wax aboard the International Space Station, with a fan blowing air past them at different speeds. In many tests the crew then applied nitrogen gas, a non-reactive extinguishing agent, until the flame went out. The goal was to learn how materials burn in weightlessness and whether ground flammability tests capture that.

technical.text: Solid fuels were burned in the MSG on the ISS using modified SPICE hardware. A 29-gage Kanthal wire igniter started each burn, and a nozzle delivered nitrogen suppressant at 0 to 500 cc/min. There were 41 samples and 89 test points: thin SIBAL cotton-fiberglass fabric, Nomex and Ultem (12 cm by 1 and 2 cm); thick PMMA and wax-saturated fiberglass (5 cm by 1 cm by 1 and 2 mm); PMMA spheres (1 and 2 cm); and paraffin and Japan wax candles. plain.text: SAME-R heated common spacecraft materials such as Teflon, Kapton, cotton, silicone rubber and a fire-retardant foam aboard the International Space Station to measure the size of the smoke particles they release. technical.text: Reflight of SAME on the ISS (Expedition 24; flight tests July 16 to September 9, 2010, 66 test points) using the SAME hardware. Spacecraft materials (Teflon, Kapton, cotton, silicone rubber and Pyrell, an intumescent fire-retardant foam replacing DBP) were heated as pyrolyzing/smoldering smoke sources. Test conditions were broadened to higher heating temperatures and no-flow during sample heating. Diagnostics measured moments of the particle size distribution (number, diameter and mass concentration; zeroth, first and third moments) with aerosol instruments, a thermal precipitator for TEM, the GRC-built M-pass, a commercial smoke detector, and ISS and Space Shuttle smoke detectors. Post-flight ground tests, including an SMPS, assessed the lognormal assumption behind the moment method. O2, pressure and flow speeds are not stated.

investigations.title: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment

plain.text: SAME heated spacecraft materials such as Teflon, Kapton, cellulose and silicone rubber aboard the International Space Station until they gave off smoke, then measured how large the smoke particles grew without gravity. The goal was to check whether the smoke detectors used on the Space Shuttle and the station would still raise an alarm for this smoke.

technical.text: Smoke from overheated (pyrolyzing/smoldering) spacecraft materials (Teflon, Kapton, cellulose, silicone rubber) was generated in the ISS Glovebox with the Comparitive Soot Diagnostic Hardware. An igniter was energized for 15 to 60 seconds, and combustion events typically lasted 2 minutes. Sample temperature, air flow and smoke residence (aging) time were test variables. Thermophoretic samplers collected particulate for post-flight TEM sizing of primary and aggregate particles, and samples were weighed for mass loss. Responses of an ionization smoke detector (Space Shuttle) and a photoelectric smoke detector (ISS) were transcribed from video. The hypothesis was that reduced buoyant mixing in μg yields larger liquid smoke droplets and a lower number density than in 1-g, which could affect detector alarms. O2, pressure and flow values are not stated in the corpus.

investigations.title: Concurrent Flame Spread Modeling using Flamelet Generated Manifolds in Microgravity with Comparison to BASS Experiments using Two-Color Tomography

plain.text: This computer-modeling project developed a faster way to simulate flames spreading along solid plastic in the same direction as the airflow (concurrent flame spread) in weightlessness. Researchers checked the simulations against camera images from NASA's BASS fire experiments. The goal was a tool to predict when spacecraft materials can burn.

technical.text: Ground investigation (GRC, 2019–2021) that implemented an unsteady flamelet generated manifold (UFGM) chemistry reduction within a fully coupled fluid–solid framework for charring and ablating materials, to simulate concurrent flame spread in microgravity. Test cases followed BASS geometries: PMMA flat sheets, spheres and rods, and wax cylinders. BASS and BASS-II imagery from PSI (DSLR cameras) was post-processed with newly developed two-color tomography to reconstruct 3D soot and temperature fields. Evaluation metrics were flame geometry, temperature distribution, soot volume fraction and flame spread rate, with emphasis on the 'Goldilocks' flammability zone reported by Olson and Ferkul. The predictions were compared with a parallel NSF normal-gravity flame spread project. O2, pressure and flow speeds are not stated in the corpus.

investigations.title: Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test / Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test-2

plain.text: DAFT and DAFT-2 tested on the International Space Station whether a modified hand-held particle counter (TSI P-Trak) works in weightlessness, where gravity cannot recycle its alcohol. The device was needed for a later smoke experiment (SAME). Measurements showed lower particle levels in ISS air than on Shuttles, and larger average particles than on Earth, helping design better smoke detectors.

technical.text: No burning is described: DAFT/DAFT-2 was a risk-mitigation test for SAME, verifying on the ISS that a TSI P-Trak condensate nuclei counter, modified to recycle isopropanol by capillary action in a redesigned condenser tube and with its mercury orientation switch removed, counts aerosol correctly in microgravity. Hypothesized failure modes were clogging/obscuration by isopropanol and over-counting from optics-chamber airflow. Arizona Red Dust (ARD), aerosolized with GN2 and contained in 15-liter Mylar bags, served as the aerosol standard; P-Trak counts were compared with a DustTrak control. The fact sheet reports low ISS particulate levels relative to Shuttles and larger average particle sizes on orbit than on Earth. Oxygen, pressure and airflow conditions are not stated.

investigations.title: Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity

plain.text: A computer-simulation study of how smoke forms in space compared with on Earth. Researchers modeled tiny particles growing from vapor released by a heated sample, with and without gravity, in a setup like the SAME smoke experiments. The goal was to understand why space smoke differs, so that smoke detectors can be designed to work better.

technical.text: Ground-based numerical investigation (2017–2019, GRC; PI Sean Garrick). Formation and growth of dibutyl-phthalate (DBP) particles from pyrolysis vapor expelled by a heated sample were simulated in Earth gravity and microgravity using direct numerical simulation via a Navier-Stokes nodal approach, in a geometry similar to the SAME experiments. Two cross-flow velocities were considered, low enough that buoyancy cannot be neglected in gravity. Simulations assess the dependence of particle size distributions on thermophoresis, particle settling and flow geometry. Buoyancy-driven wake differences were examined at the lower flow speed, and instantaneous scalar fields describe particle accumulation and growth in buoyant and non-buoyant wakes. Oxygen, pressure and velocity values are not stated in the corpus.

investigations.title: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment

plain.text: SPICE burned small gas jets, similar to a lighter flame, aboard the International Space Station. The goal was to find each flame's 'smoke point', the size at which it starts releasing soot (dark carbon particles). Soot makes fires radiate heat, which helps them spread. The results inform how fires behave in spacecraft and how cabin materials are chosen.

technical.text: Laminar non-buoyant round jet diffusion flames were stabilized on nozzles of 0.41 mm, 0.76 mm and 1.6 mm diameter in co-flowing air at 5.4 cm/s to 65 cm/s. Fuels were methane, ethylene, propane, propylene and propylene mixtures. The flames burned inside a flow duct in the Microgravity Science Glovebox on the ISS. Fuel flow rate was varied to locate the laminar smoke point, the onset of soot emission. Still and video cameras recorded luminous flame lengths. Measurements included flame height, radiative heat losses and co-flow air velocity distributions. The PSI card reports 526 flames; the fact sheet reports 250 tests and more than 70 smoke points. Oxygen concentrations other than air, and pressure, are not stated.

plain.text: This ground study re-analyzed more than 1600 photos from NASA's SPICE experiment, which burned small gas-jet flames (like a lighter flame) in microgravity. It combined the images with computer models to study soot, the dark carbon particles that make flames glow and give off heat, and to understand why flames form soot differently in weightlessness than on Earth.

technical.text: Ground investigation (Yale; PI Smooke) that integrated experiments and computation on the SPICE laminar coflow gas-jet diffusion flame data sets in PSI. investigations.title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

plain.text: This ground study used computer simulations to understand 'cool flames': faint, low-temperature flames that can surround burning fuel droplets in weightlessness. Using data from the space station's FLEX experiment, it tested how added heat and gentle air motion change whether these flames start, pulse, turn into hot flames, or go out.

technical.text: Ground CFD investigation (PI Tanvir Farouk) of n-alkane droplet cool flames in microgravity. A 3-D OpenFOAM model couples variable-density Navier–Stokes flow, low-temperature combustion chemistry, coupled heat and mass transfer, and radiation, with fidelity established against ISS FLEX measurements. Three forcing modes were simulated on large (1–4 mm) and sub-millimeter (~0.5 mm) droplets: convection alone (mimicking droplet drift), imposed heat flux, and combined convection plus heating. Work began with simplified chemistry and moved to reduced mechanisms for sweeps over forcing amplitude and frequency, ambient composition (including ozone-assisted cases) and pressure. Ignition delay, oscillation frequency and amplitude, and stand-off and extinction diameters were extracted to build stability maps for cool-flame onset, persistence and quenching, which were reconciled with FLEX observations.

plain.text: FLEX-2 burned tiny liquid fuel droplets aboard the International Space Station. Without gravity, each flame forms a ball around its droplet. investigations.title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design

plain.text: Flame Design burned ethylene and methane gas from a ball-shaped porous burner aboard the International Space Station. Without gravity the flames form spheres. The goal was to learn when soot (carbon particles) starts forming and when flames go out, so that clean, efficient flames can be designed. The team also tested whether flammability limits can be found for these flames.

Variables were flow rate, stoichiometric mixture fraction Zst, inert amount (N2 or CO2) and pressure, with oxygen-enriched atmospheres. Methane and ethylene, usually diluted with nitrogen, are the shared fuels: BRE uses CH4/N2 and C2H4/N2, and Flame Design, CLD Flame and E-FIELD use methane and ethylene. s-Flame uses H2/CH4 and C2H4 mixtures. CFI-G is the exception, burning propane, n-butane and n-pentane.

Extinction is a common target. BRE reduces fuel flow until the flame goes out. Flame Design and s-Flame seek radiative versus kinetic or convective extinction limits. CLD Flame and E-FIELD dilute flames down to near-extinction. CFI-G lowers flow toward extinction of cool flames.

Burners are shared within the family. Flame Design, CFI-G and s-Flame use a porous spherical burner, which gives nominally one-dimensional spherical flames. E-FIELD reuses the CLD Flame coflow burner, and Flame Design lists coflow as an alternative configuration.

Fuel mixtures were chosen to match heat of combustion, smoke point and heat of gasification, and they were fed through a flat porous burner of 25 or 50 mm diameter carrying heat flux transducers and a surface thermocouple. It alone states three atmospheres: 21% O2 at 14.7 psia, 26.5% at 10.2 psia and 34% at 8.2 psia. Its record reports sustained burning without airflow only in the elevated-oxygen atmospheres.

It also varies the inert diluent (N2 or CO2), pressure, and normal versus inverse configurations (an inverse flame issues oxidizer from the burner). It targets soot-inception and extinction limits and tests the hypothesis that spherical flames go out when peak temperature first drops below 1130 K.

ACME CLD Flame studies lifted coflow jet flames, varying fuel injection velocity and nitrogen dilution from sooting to near-extinction flames, with normal-gravity comparisons. It is the only ACME record here with findings: microgravity sooty flames held five to eight times more soot, and dilute microgravity flames stayed stable at lower fuel concentrations.

ACME E-FIELD Flames adds an electric field. A copper mesh electrode placed about 35 or 50 mm downstream was set between +10 and -10 kV, and the investigation varied field strength, polarity and electrode position while measuring voltage-current curves of the flame's ions. ACME CFI-G targets cool diffusion flames (peak temperatures of 500 to 1000 K) of propane, n-butane and n-pentane. It studies their extinction at reduced flow and their transition to hot flames at increased flow. Engine efficiency is its stated motivation.

ACME s-Flame varies diluent type and placement (nitrogen and helium to change diffusivity, CO2 to change radiation) in both the fuel and the chamber. The group splits by fuel. BASS and BASS-II burn solid samples with flow along the surface in concurrent (same direction as spread) or opposed directions. SPICE and SLICE burn gaseous jet flames from exchangeable nozzles in a coflow of air.

differences.text: BASS is the broadest materials survey: 41 samples and 89 test points. Materials were SIBAL cotton-fiberglass fabric, Nomex, Ultem, PMMA slabs and 1 and 2 cm spheres, wax-saturated fiberglass, and paraffin and Japan-wax candles. It alone adds a nozzle of nitrogen suppressant at 0 to 500 cc/min and varies ignition location on spheres.

BASS-II adds oxygen as a variable by lowering it below 21% through nitrogen vitiation (diluting the working volume with nitrogen). It burns acrylic films, sheets, rods and a large spherical section. Its record reports a thin-to-thick fuel transition formula and model spread rates higher than observed.

SPICE varies gaseous fuel (methane, ethylene, propane, propylene and mixtures), nozzle diameter (0.41, 0.76 and 1.6 mm), co-flow speed (5.4 to 65 cm/s) and fuel flow. The aim is to locate the smoke point, the onset of soot emission; more than 70 smoke points were reported.

SLICE burns methane, ethylene and their nitrogen dilutions. It holds fuel flow fixed and raises air velocity until the flame lifts off the nozzle, recording more than 4,000 still images over 13 testing experiments. Its record describes it as a precursor to ACME CLD Flame.

hardware_groups.name: Saffire large-scale tests aboard Cygnus
hardware_groups.hardware: Saffire flow-duct enclosure (fans, flow straighteners, central sample card) in the Cygnus vehicle after it deberthed from the ISS

similarities.text: All three burn samples on a card in the middle of a large fan-driven air duct, uncrewed, after Cygnus left the ISS. They share the same diagnostics: two cameras, thermocouples, two radiometers, solid-state sensors for pressure, CO2 and O2, and two anemometers.

All three share the objectives of measuring large-scale low-gravity fire growth rate and comparing low-gravity flammability limits with NASA's normal-gravity material screening test. No ambient O2 or pressure set-points and no measured findings appear in the records.

differences.text: Saffire-I burned a single large SIBAL fabric sheet, about 0.94 m by 0.4 m, at one air speed of 20 cm/s.

Saffire-II burned nine smaller samples, each 5 cm by 29 cm, of SIBAL, silicone, structure PMMA, flat PMMA and PMMA with Nomex. Air speed was 20 or 30 cm/s, concurrent or opposed depending on material. It is the only one of the three to vary material.
Saffire-III returned to SIBAL at a higher flow of 30 cm/s, concurrent or opposed. Its sample dimensions are not stated.

hardware_groups.name: SAME smoke-detection hardware in the Glovebox
hardware_groups.hardware: Comparative Soot Diagnostic Hardware in the ISS Glovebox, with spacecraft smoke detectors and thermophoretic samplers

similarities.text: Both heat spacecraft materials (Teflon, Kapton, silicone rubber, and cellulose or cotton) until they pyrolyze or smolder. They then measure the resulting smoke with thermophoretic sampling for electron-microscope (TEM) sizing and with ISS and Space Shuttle smoke detectors, and both compare un-aged and aged smoke.
Neither record states oxygen, pressure or flow-speed values, and neither reports measured particle sizes or detector responses.

differences.text: SAME varies igniter on-time (15 to 60 s) and determines 1-g conditions with the same mass loss, for comparison with flight. It tests the hypothesis that weaker mixing in microgravity yields larger smoke droplets at lower number density, which could affect alarms.

SAME-R (66 test points, Expedition 24) adds cotton and Pyrell, a fire-retardant foam that its record says replaced SAME's DBP samples. It extends tests to higher heating temperatures and to no-flow heating, and swaps in the GRC-built M-pass instrument. Its size moments rely on a lognormal assumption that was checked in post-flight ground tests.

hardware_groups.name: Other
hardware_groups.hardware: No shared flight hardware: an aerosol-instrument test (DAFT) and ground computational or laboratory studies that reuse flight data from other investigations

similarities.text: Each builds on another investigation in this ranking: DAFT was a risk-mitigation test for SAME, PSI-115 simulates a SAME-like geometry, PSI-62 post-processes BASS and BASS-II imagery, PSI-60 analyzes SPICE images, and PSI-117 and PSI-142 use FLEX flight data.
None of them produced new microgravity combustion measurements: DAFT burned nothing, and the other five are ground investigations.

differences.text: DAFT verified on the ISS that a modified P-Trak particle counter works in microgravity, comparing it with a DustTrak, using Arizona Red Dust and cabin air. It reports low ISS particulate levels and larger on-orbit particle sizes.

PSI-62 simulates concurrent flame spread over PMMA sheets, spheres and rods and over wax cylinders, using a reduced-chemistry (flamelet) model coupled to the solid. It reconstructs 3D soot and temperature fields from BASS/BASS-II camera images by two-color tomography.

PSI-115 numerically simulates DBP smoke-particle formation in Earth gravity versus microgravity at two low cross-flow speeds. It assesses how thermophoresis, settling and geometry shape particle size distributions.
PSI-60 decoded over 1600 SPICE DSLR images into soot temperature and volume fraction fields. It compared them with a soot model for Yale and ACME burners in normal and microgravity.

PSI-117 is a 3-D CFD model of n-alkane droplet cool flames, validated against FLEX. It sweeps drift-like convection, heat flux, droplet size, ambient composition and pressure to build cool-flame stability maps.

PSI-142 uses ground counterflow flames sensitized with ozone, plus modeling of n-heptane and DME, to map cool-flame extinction under FLEX conditions. It studies elevated pressure up to 20 atm rather than reduced pressure.

gaps.text: No record reports partial-gravity combustion tests. FLEX, FLEX-2 and ACME-BRE state microgravity only, and E-FIELD reports no explicitly simulated partial gravity. The closest bounding data are paired microgravity and normal-gravity comparisons in CLD Flame, SLICE and several ground studies.

Elevated oxygen at reduced pressure, the expected Moon-base and rover atmosphere, is stated only for ACME-BRE, and there with gaseous emulators of solids. The real solid-material tests either give no oxygen set-point or only lower oxygen below 21% (BASS-II). Saffire-II's record attributes varied-oxygen and varied-pressure tests to Saffire IV, which is not in this ranking.

Test-level suppression data exist only for FLEX, which tested CO2 and helium on liquid droplets. On solids, the only suppressant described is BASS's nitrogen nozzle, with no flight results in its record. No record describes any other suppression agent.

The detection pillar rests on smoke and aerosol work whose records contain no measured particle sizes or detector responses (SAME, SAME-R). The remaining detection entries are an instrument check that burned nothing (DAFT) and a purely numerical study (PSI-115). None states the oxygen or pressure of the smoke tests.
Five investigations rest only on their summary card and PSI record, with no fact sheet or papers. One of them, CFI, is a flight experiment, and its pressure range is internally inconsistent.

Only FLEX has data rated ready for modeling. Every other combustion investigation needs extraction, including the flame-spread flights BASS, BASS-II and Saffire-I to -III, whose records hold no test-level results. Source discrepancies would also need resolving: airflow is given as up to 40 cm/s versus 5 to 50 cm/s for BASS, and SPICE reports 526 flames versus 250 tests.
